unit-m3u5.title: Unit 3 · Lesson 5: Multiply 3-Digit by 2-Digit Numbers
unit-m3u5.source: enVision Topic 3 textbook scan — Multiply Multi-Digit Whole Numbers (Drive)

summary.text: Lesson 3-5 of the Topic 3 textbook scan: multiplying a 3-digit number by a 2-digit number with partial products and the standard algorithm.

why.text: This is the biggest multiplication she does in this unit, and it is exactly the same two-row method with a longer row.

objectives.text: Multiply 3-digit by 2-digit numbers with the standard algorithm
Use estimation to check that a product is reasonable
Know the most digits a 3-digit × 2-digit product can have

parentNote.text: The mistake that matters most here is the missing placeholder zero, and it is easy to catch: the answer comes out roughly ten times too small. Several wrong options are built from exactly that slip (247 × 36 → 2,223), and one question asks her to spot it with an estimate alone. The digit-count rule — never more than 5 digits — is a quick extra check the book mentions in its assessment practice.

nextUp.text: Same two rows, longer numbers. Estimate first so you know the size.

cards.def:
**Multiplying a 3-digit number by a 2-digit number uses the same two rows as before.**
• Row 1: the whole top number × the ones digit.
• Row 2: the whole top number × the tens digit, starting with a 0.
• Add the rows.
cards.hint: Nothing new — just a longer row.

cards.def:
**The area model has six pieces: hundreds, tens and ones of one factor times tens and ones of the other.**
• You can list all six or let the standard algorithm combine them.
cards.hint: Three parts × two parts = six pieces.

cards.term: How many digits can the product have?
cards.def:
**A 3-digit number times a 2-digit number has at most 5 digits.**
• The biggest case is 999 × 99 = 98,901.
cards.hint: Handy for spotting an answer with too many or too few digits.

cards.def:
**Round both factors and multiply.**
• 386 × 17 is about 400 × 20 = 8,000, or closer: 400 × 17 = 6,800.
cards.hint: An answer ten times too big or too small almost always means a lost or extra zero.

questions.q: To find 247 × 36 with the standard algorithm, what do you multiply first?
questions.hint: The standard algorithm always starts with the ones digit of the bottom number.

ex.main: **247 × 6.** Row 1 is the whole top number times the ones digit.
ex.tip: The second row will be 247 × 30 — the 3 means 3 tens.
2,223 leaves the zero off the second row; 7,410 and 1,482 are each only one row.
Estimate: 500 × 24 = 12,000. 3,108 is far too small — a missing placeholder zero.
3,088 adds 386 × 7 and 386 × 1 — the 1 in 17 means 1 ten. 3,860 is only one row.

questions.q: A cat's heart beats about 146 times a minute. How many times does it beat in 1 hour?
questions.hint: There are 60 minutes in an hour.

ex.tip: 206 comes from adding 146 and 60. "Each minute for 60 minutes" means multiply.

questions.q: A garden store packs 8 plants in a tray and 6 trays in a flat. It sold 23 flats on Saturday and 19 on Sunday. How many plants did it sell?
questions.hint: Find the plants in one flat and the number of flats first.

ex.tip: 1,104 counts only Saturday. 336 multiplies 8 × 42 and forgets the trays.

questions.q: A patio is 126 bricks wide and 23 bricks long. How many bricks does it take?
questions.hint: Multiply the width by the length.

ex.tip: 149 is 126 + 23 — the bricks fill a rectangle, so multiply.
